https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/07.title: Mother of jailed Just Stop Oil activist, 22, says sentence means she’ll miss brother’s wedding
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/07.subtitle: Cathy Gethin says her daughter Cressida, imprisoned for four years alongside Extinction Rebellion co-founder, ‘has courage of a lion’
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/07.text:
The mother of a 22-year-old Just Stop Oil activist who was jailed for four years has said her daughter will miss her brother’s wedding while imprisoned.
Cressida Gethin, 22 was jailed alongside Roger Hallam, the co-founder of Extinction Rebellion, and three other activists following a Just Stop Oil campaign on the M25 over four days of disruption in November 2022.
Hallam, 58, was found guilty of conspiring to block traffic and given a record five-year prison sentence after a judge ruled he had “crossed the line from concerned campaigner to fanatic”.
Each of the other activists – Lucia Whittaker De Abreu, 34, Daniel Shaw, 38, Louise Lancaster, 58, and Gethin – were last week given four-year sentences after they were found guilty of conspiring to block traffic on the M25.
Cathy Gethin gave a speech following the sentencing and said: “My daughter is Cressida Gethin. At the age of 22 she was the youngest defendant, and she has just been sentenced today to four years in prison. This means she will not be present at her brother’s wedding next summer.
“Cressida grew up in the countryside and is one of those nature-loving defendants that you’ve heard about. She’s an extremely talented musician. She worked hard growing up, she achieved highly. She has ambitions, dreams and hopes, like all young people.
“[Cressida] had just finished her first year at university. Cressida also grew up completely understanding right and wrong. She has always been unable to stand by when she sees injustice. She has the courage of a lion and a moral compass that compels her to step forward when she sees wrong and what she has seen, what so many people will not face is that our leaders are sleepwalking us to a climate apocalypse by their failure to prioritise decarbonisation and that with this will come enormous suffering.”
Ms Gethin added: “When she had the science and saw that no one was paying attention, she felt she had no option.
“In 2022 when she was 20 years old, she took to direct action and engaged in civil resistance, a strategy with proven results, albeit with risks for those who step up. She now faces a multi-year sentence in prison.”
The Attorney General was under pressure to intervene over the sentences given to Mr Hallam, who also set up Just Stop Oil, and his co-conspirators, which are the longest for non-violent protest in living memory.
Despite being welcomed by Tory MPs, the sentences were widely condemned by celebrities including Chris Packham and Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall and green campaigners including Labour’s biggest corporate donor.
Southwark Crown Court had heard each of the defendants had recruited activists over a Zoom call to take part in the motorway demonstration, which the prosecution said had caused economic damage of nearly £750,000 and cost the police £1 million.
The protests unfolded over four days from November 7, with 45 activists climbing up different gantries across the M25.
Hallam and the fellow defendants were prosecuted under a new law of conspiracy intentionally to cause a public nuisance introduced by the last Tory government in an attempt to crack down on disruptive protests.
The five protest organisers were convicted of conspiracy to intentionally cause a public nuisance. The court heard they organised “height training”, teaching activists how to climb motorway gantries. They also rehearsed a “blue lights policy” to let police pass on the motorway.
The disruption is said to have caused more than 50,000 hours of traffic delay, affecting the journeys of more than 700,000 vehicles. Two lorries collided and an Essex police officer suffered concussion and bruising after he was knocked off his motorbike in traffic.
The sentences exceeded those handed out in 2023 to two other Just Stop Oil activists who were jailed for climbing the Queen Elizabeth II bridge on the Dartford Crossing.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/07.title:
What has Britain done? Labour is 
already showing its sinister true colours
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/07.subtitle: Starmer has only been in office for one week, and the terrible decisions are starting to add up
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/07.text:
We are only one week into the new Government and, in thoroughly British fashion, the appalling decisions are already forming an orderly queue. Sir Keir Starmer won a little over a third of the vote, and yet the Prime Minister now commands a majority of 172 and can enact any policy he pleases. He’s seized the opportunity – and in the process is demonstrating that this is going to be a government far more Left-wing, and far more willing to make terrible choices, than many people had perhaps anticipated.
If you only watched the broadcast media, or read the liberal press, you would think that everything is sunlight and optimism. They are too busy salivating over Saint Starmer and his Cabinet of “decency”, as one activist masquerading as a journalist sycophantically put it on social media, to bother with any form of scrutiny. They speak of a new administration that has “hit the ground running” and, while some of health secretary Wes Streeting’s signals on NHS reform – and Defence Secretary John Healey’s swift visit to Ukraine – should be welcomed, it doesn’t exactly look as if things can only get better.
Take the return of Ed Miliband, whose past reputation as a political laughing stock, with his Ed Stone and inability to eat a bacon sandwich, has been curiously forgotten. In his new role as Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero, he has already shown that is willing to embrace the sort of Extinction Rebellion-esque dogma the country has come to despise.
As this newspaper reported, Miliband has ordered an immediate ban on drilling in new North Sea oil fields, having overruled Energy Department officials to intervene in what is usually an apolitical process. He has decreed that regulators will not approve a round of drilling in new oil fields that was slated for confirmation in the coming weeks. This means that companies will have wasted millions of pounds on preparing their bids, and experts are warning that they are likely to take legal action as a result.
In what world is this good governance? Even under net zero, there will be a need for oil and gas. I’m not usually prone to quoting union bosses, but Sharon Graham, Unite general secretary, hit the nail on the head when she said this week: “It is quite frankly irresponsible for Labour to keep ploughing ahead with the guillotine ban of new oil and gas licences when there is no clear plan for jobs. We simply cannot let go of one rope before we have hold of another. Until we have clear plans and more importantly investment, we should not be turning off the taps. In a less stable world, we cannot rely on imports nor offshore our carbon responsibilities.”
There’s a time and a place for ordering an immediate ban on drilling in new North Sea oil fields, Ed, and it isn’t when Russia is still at war with Ukraine, the British economy is in chaos – to quote new Chancellor Rachel Reeves – and 78.4 per cent of the UK’s energy still comes from fossil fuels. Forget the Ed Stone, Miliband appears intent on carving out a national suicide note.
Far from inspiring confidence, the decision to appoint lockdown-loving Sir Patrick Vallance as science minister and Chris Stark, former head of the Climate Change Committee, to lead “Mission Control” to deliver clean power by 2030, appears to have been made in an eco echo chamber. Are there any dissenting voices within government and the Civil Service on whether decarbonising the grid in six years is even feasible, let alone affordable? (Chief Secretary to the Treasury Darren Jones’s admission that Labour’s green plans will cost “hundreds of billions” suggests probably not).
The decision to release thousands of prisoners early is another sign of impending doom. Responding to a question about prison overcrowding at the Nato summit in Washington DC on Thursday night, Starmer reminded everyone that he “worked in criminal justice” (he was a former director of public prosecutions, don’t you know?) before adding: “We knew there was going to be a problem, but the scale of the problem was worse than we thought.”
Really? That’s odd, because it was only in May that the former lawyer quizzed Rishi Sunak – in detail – about the issue at Prime Minister’s Questions, when he demanded a guarantee that “none of the criminals… released early are high risk”. We now learn that Justice Secretary Shabana Mahmood plans to free criminals, including some convicted of violence, just 40 per cent of the way through their sentence rather than the current halfway point.
As with the state of the nation’s finances – upon which Labour has been providing a running commentary for the past 14 years – it’s no secret that our prison service is in a shockingly bad state. Only last month, a riot erupted in Parc jail in Bridgend in Labour-run Wales. Indeed, the party’s 2024 manifesto commits to “tackling the prisons crisis”, adding: “The Conservatives’ failure to build sufficient places has led to overcrowding and chaos.” So I’m not quite sure why Starmer is treating it as an issue Labour has only just discovered. The reality is they’ve had months, if not years, to anticipate what they might do to avert this disaster.
Bizarrely, despite us having far too few prison spaces, Starmer wants to scrap the Legacy Act, which is intended to stop soldiers involved in the Troubles from being hauled through the courts. Quite how prosecuting a load of ageing Northern Ireland veterans helps is anyone’s guess.
Meanwhile, the Rwanda plan has been scrapped without a replacement. Labour claims that its new border security command will “stop the boats”, but Starmer cannot seem to find anyone to run it after his first choice Neil Basu, the UK’s former head of counter-terrorism, apparently declined the offer to apply for the role. The problem of people arriving illegally across the Channel only seems to be getting worse, with newly-released Home Office figures showing 419 people made the journey in six boats on Tuesday, taking the provisional total for 2024 to date to 14,058. This is 10 per cent higher than the number recorded this time last year (12,772) and up 6 per cent on the same period in 2022 (13,318).
And in other news, Anneliese Dodds has been appointed women and equalities minister – and will now be in charge of Labour’s controversial conversion therapy ban – despite once suggesting that defining what a woman is “does depend what the context is.” Oh and the Prime Minister doesn’t think Joe Biden is “senile”, despite him confusing President Zelensky with President Putin and thinking Donald Trump is his vice-president. To think they’re only just getting started.
We’ve got at least four more years of this.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/07.title: Extinction Rebellion founder jailed for five years
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/07.subtitle: Roger Hallam handed record sentence after being found guilty of conspiring to block traffic on the M25
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/07.text:
The founder of Extinction Rebellion has been jailed for five years in what is believed to be the longest sentence for non-violent protest in the UK.
Roger Hallam was found guilty of conspiring to block traffic as part of a Just Stop Oil campaign on the M25 over four days of disruption in November 2022.
Four other activists were given four-year sentences for the protests, in which demonstrators climbed the gantry above the motorway and displayed Just Stop Oil banners.
The court heard that each of the defendants had recruited activists over a Zoom call to take part in the demonstration, which the prosecution said had caused economic damage of nearly £750,000 and cost the police £1 million.
Daniel Shaw, 38, from Northampton, Lucia Whittaker De Abreu, 34, from Derby, Louise Lancaster, 58, from Cambridge, and Cressida Gethin, 22, from Hereford, were all sentenced to four years in prison.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/07.title: Progressive parents have brought up a generation of entitled, selfish brats
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/07.subtitle: Teaching children that the world revolves around them and their whims lays the groundwork for their future careers as activists
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/07.text:
It’s not hard to poke fun at today’s cohort of climate activists. The sheer number of double-barrelled names makes writing jokes feel too easy. But what isn’t so funny is watching the whining from these posh protesters when faced with the consequences of their actions.
I am die-hard when it comes to the freedom to protest. I’d like to see the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act repealed and the talk of buffer zones around political offices squashed. It’s outrageous that citizens now have to prove to police officers that they’re being the right level of “noisy” to freely challenge our political leaders.
I even think five years for the Just Stop Oil brigade is too harsh – setting a dangerous precedent for the future of political disruption. It’s the kind of sentence that could be used against protests that I might want to join in the future, for Brexit or child benefits or anything.
But – and it’s a big but – the arrogance of the Just Stop Oil brigade’s response to their punishment has been staggering. These people are “truth tellers”, we’re told, and should be applauded rather than jailed for lying across motorways and chucking orange gunk on the nation’s artefacts.
“We are the enlightened ones”, they cry, “we wouldn’t be doing this kind of thing if we weren’t sure that everyone should do what we say”. “I am a doctor” one activist shouted at me on an episode of Politics Live on the BBC this afternoon. This isn’t just elitism, it’s authoritarian madness.
The extent of this feeling of entitlement was really brought home by a statement made by the mother of one of the protesters – Cressida Gethin. In a speech to protesters, Cathy from Herefordshire pleaded with the crowd for sympathy: “She has just been sentenced today to four years in prison. This means she will not be present at her brother’s wedding next summer.” Sound the orchestra of tiny violins: Cressida – whose organisation seeks to bring the nation to a standstill – won’t be able to go to the ball.
You have to wonder what message this sends to the youthful audience that the likes of Just Stop Oil and Extinction Rebellion seem to target. Their supporters are predominantly made up of people who don’t have many responsibilities – either school kids or retired vicars, neither likely to have to worry about getting to work.
The lionisation of these serial disruptors tells young people that they too can become saints, if they only chain themselves to something annoying. Better still, Cathy’s plea for sympathy for her daughter tells them that even when they really upset people, they shouldn’t worry too much about the consequences. Rowan Williams and his posse will be there to demand that they’re bailed out.
This so-called progressive, gentle, middle-class parenting is creating a generation of spoilt brats. Much has been made of Cressida Gethin’s status as a “Cambridge graduate”. There’s a reason there aren’t many plasterer’s daughters among Just Stop Oil, working-class parents still thankfully have some sense of social responsibility.
We’re less likely to bring our kids up to think the world revolves around them and their activist whims because, well, it doesn’t. From schools celebrating their children marching around like mini Greta Thunbergs to the demands from climate graduates that they’re sick of “polite” methods of public engagement, kids are being turned into megalomaniac monsters.
Contrary to the claims of privileged twenty-somethings, the way out of the challenges we face in relation to a changing climate is not through iconoclasm and luddite policy measures. We will not fix the planet by making people’s lives a misery.
We need to teach our kids that political quandaries are never black and white, good or evil, and that democracy demands you win popular support for your cause rather than seeking to override public sentiment. Most importantly, the adults in the room need to reassert that we might know a little better than spoilt, overgrown children, who think throwing their toys out of their eco prams is the way to change the world.
